name: Shortest Plans: Ladder
description: A ten-level difficulty ladder of one planning task: the fewest moves that bring every disk of a scattered four-peg Tower of Hanoi onto peg D. Only the number of disks grows, from 4 (256 positions, a 6-move minimum) to 13 (67 million positions, a 70-move minimum), so every level is strictly more search than the one below. The answer is the proven minimum, so the model must both find a short plan and rule out every shorter one; each minimum is proven by breadth-first search over every position and re-proved by an independent search.
hook: From 6 moves to 70: how deep can it plan before one move too many?
author: Gauntlet Core

cases.prompt:
There are four pegs, A, B, C and D, and four disks of different sizes numbered 1 (smallest) to 4 (largest).

Current position (each peg listed from the bottom up):
- Peg A: disk 3 only.
- Peg B: disk 4 at the bottom with disk 1 on top of it.
- Peg C: disk 2 only.
- Peg D: empty.

A move consists of taking the top disk from any peg and placing it on top of another peg. A disk may never be placed on top of a smaller disk.

What is the minimum number of moves needed to get all four disks onto peg D?

Give the answer as a single integer (digits only, no units). Give exactly one answer. If you give more than one answer, it will be marked wrong.
cases.notes: [level 1] 4 disks on four pegs: 4^4 = 256 positions, proven minimum 6 moves. Breadth-first search over every position (numpy, plans_ladder/hanoi.py) gives the exact distance of every position to the goal; this start was drawn (seed 4101) among the 66 positions exactly 6 moves away, with the largest disk not yet on peg D and disks on at least three pegs. The same search re-proves the known four-peg minima for a full tower (here 9 moves from peg A, the farthest any position is from the goal: 9). Independently re-proved by plans_ladder/verify.mjs, a forward breadth-first search in JavaScript from the position parsed out of this prompt. Ladder: ten frozen levels (L01 easiest, L10 hardest) of the same task under the same rules; only the size grows. Every level is worth the same, so the test score is the share of the ladder climbed; the headline is the highest level solved reliably. One optimal plan: disk 1 B to A; disk 4 B to D; disk 1 A to B; disk 3 A to D; disk 2 C to D; disk 1 B to D.
